What this is about A computer that is supposed to learn something from data sees no apartments, no texts and no images. It sees only numbers. Before we can talk about learning methods, it must therefore be clear how to describe a thing from the real world by numbers and which calculations with these numbers make sense. This chapter pursues the question of how to write down many measured values of many things so that you can calculate with them how to measure how similar two things are and how far apart they lie, how to turn several measured values into a single estimate and how to apply the same calculation to a thousand things at once. On top of that comes the question of when such a calculation destroys information and when it can be undone. The payoff the chapter establishes the language in which all further parts of the series are written. Once you master it, you can read every later method as a calculation with lists and tables of numbers. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why a method works and where it comes from , derivations and proofs; you do not need them to read on. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first and actually run the programs; the solution expands right below each exercise.

This calculation is the most common one in all of machine learning it turns measured values into an estimate and compares data with a pattern. Weights and weighted sums A real estate agent estimates the price of an apartment in her head roughly like this each square meter is worth about thousand euros, each room adds another thousand euros, and each kilometer of distance from the center takes off thousand euros. So she takes each feature with its own factor and adds everything up. The number with which a feature enters such a calculation is called its weight . A large positive weight means that each unit of this feature raises the result strongly. A negative weight means that the feature lowers the result. For a vector of weights and an example , the weighted sum is A fixed rule that computes a number from the features of an example is called a model . The number that the model returns for an example is called its prediction . The hat over the in indicates that this is a computed estimate and not a measured value. In this chapter the weights are always given; where good weights come from is a question of its own. The dot product as a comparison with a pattern The outdoor temperature is read every twelve hours, alternately at noon and at midnight. Four consecutive values form a vector, here called a time series . Each value is multiplied by the pattern value at the same position. If the time series has the same sign as the pattern at a position, the product is positive; if it has the opposite sign, the product is negative. If the time series follows the pattern everywhere, only positive contributions add up to a large sum. Cross correlation compares a sequence with a pattern not just at one position but for every possible shift. For each shift , its value is a dot product the sequence with the pattern shifted by positions. So the whole correlation function is a sequence of dot products, one per shift. How large is a vector? There are several correct answers to this question. This section presents the three most important ones, clarifies what they have in common and shows what they are needed for to measure how large an error is. The Euclidean norm The obvious size of an arrow is its length. In the plane, the Pythagorean theorem gives it the arrow is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs and , so its length is . In space you apply Pythagoras twice and get the square root of the sum of the three squares. The same formula is used in every dimension. The Euclidean norm of a vector is Without a subscript, in this series always means the Euclidean norm. It is also called the length of the vector or, because of the squares, the norm. A vector of length is called normalized . If you divide a vector by its length, then is normalized and points in the same direction. This step is called normalizing . The vector has length Fig. 12 abb 12 . Normalized, it is . In space, . The Euclidean norm of square the components, add, take the square root. The minus sign disappears when squaring. ⁠ In short The Euclidean norm is the length of the arrow, the square root of the sum of the squared components. The 1 norm In a city with a rectangular street grid, a taxi cannot drive diagonally through the blocks. To get from the origin to the point , it drives blocks in one direction and blocks in the other, blocks in total. The 1 norm measures this length. The 1 norm of a vector is It is also called the norm or, after the street grid of Manhattan, the Manhattan norm. For , Fig. 13 abb 13 , and . The 1 norm of add the absolute values of the components. Here the 1 norm is larger than the Euclidean length, because the detour along the streets is longer than the straight line. ⁠ In short The 1 norm adds the absolute values of the components; it is the route through a rectangular street grid. The maximum norm In a quality inspection, often only the worst deviation matters. A part has three dimensions, and each may deviate from its nominal value by at most mm. Whether the part passes is decided by the largest of the three deviations alone. The maximum norm of a vector is the largest absolute value of a component It is also called the norm. The reason for the infinity symbol is given in the next subsection. and . If the deviations of a part are mm, their maximum norm is mm, and the part passes. ⁠ In short The maximum norm is the largest absolute value of a component, the worst single deviation. What makes a norm The three norms measure differently, but they share three properties that you expect from any measure of size. Only the zero vector has size zero. A vector twice as long is twice as large. And a detour is never shorter than the direct route. A dataset consists of many vectors with the same number of components. This section combines them into a single table of numbers, a matrix, and establishes how to write and calculate with matrices. Matrices The table of apartments is more than four separate vectors it is one object that you want to calculate with as a whole. A grayscale image is also a table, namely of brightness values, arranged in rows and columns. Such a rectangular array of numbers is called a matrix. A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of real numbers in rows and columns The number in row and column is called an entry of the matrix. The pair is called the size of the matrix. Matrices are written in bold capital letters, their entries with the corresponding lowercase letter and two indices first the row, then the column. The th column of is a vector with components; it is called . The matrix is then also written as a row of its columns, . A vector with components is a matrix of size , and a row with numbers is a matrix of size . Two matrices are equal if they have the same size and the same entry in every position. Matrices of the same size are added and multiplied by a number entry by entry, just like vectors and . The matrix has size , the entries and , and the second column . A grayscale image of pixels that shows a bright cross on a dark background is the matrix with the rows , and . Furthermore, ⁠ In short A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers with rows and columns; the entry is in row and column . If you read out an image row by row and string the rows together, the matrix becomes a long vector the cross becomes the vector , and a image becomes a vector in . The numbers stay the same, but one piece of information is lost in this notation which pixels are neighbors. The pixel directly below another one is positions further back in the long vector. For calculations that weight each feature individually, this does not matter. For calculations that want to exploit neighborhoods, the matrix form is the more natural one. Square matrices and diagonal matrices Some matrices occur so often that they have their own names. In all three cases the shape of the table is particularly simple. A matrix with the same number of rows and columns is called square . The entries of a square matrix form its diagonal , which runs from the top left to the bottom right. A square matrix whose entries off the diagonal are all zero is called a diagonal matrix . For a vector , is the diagonal matrix with the diagonal entries . The matrix whose entries are all zero is called the zero matrix and is written . The second matrix has a diagonal entry zero and is still a diagonal matrix; the only requirement is that all entries off the diagonal are zero. What this is about In Chapter 1 /wissen/en/informatik/machine learning/mathematische grundlagen/vektoren und matrizen/vektoren und matrizen.html one question was left open. Four apartments are described by their floor area and their number of rooms, and their prices are known. We are looking for two weights with which the weighted sum hits every price. Such weights do not exist four equations in two unknowns contradict one another. With measured data this is almost always the case. You have more measurements than unknowns, every measurement is slightly inaccurate, and the system of equations has no solution. Still, you need weights, namely the ones that are off by as little as possible. This chapter pursues this question and two more that turn out to be closely related. Are there directions in which a matrix only makes an arrow longer or shorter without rotating it, and what do these directions reveal about the matrix? And can every matrix be split into a few simple building blocks, ordered by importance, so that the unimportant ones can be left out? On top of that comes a practical question how much does the result of a calculation change when the data are slightly wrong? The payoff with the answers, you fit a line or another simple rule to measured values so that the error is as small as possible. You can tell whether a function of several variables has a hollow, a ridge or a saddle. You approximate an image or a large table with a few numbers and know how much is lost in the process. And you can judge whether a computed result can be trusted. The tools of this chapter show up in almost all later parts of the series. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why a method works and where it comes from , derivations and proofs; you do not need them to read on. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first and actually run the programs; the solution expands right below each exercise.

What this is about A number often depends on many other numbers. The price that the weighted sum from Chapter 1 /wissen/en/informatik/machine learning/mathematische grundlagen/vektoren und matrizen/vektoren und matrizen.html predicts for an apartment depends on every weight and every feature. The length of an error vector depends on each of its components. The result of a long calculation depends on every value it starts with. This chapter asks how strongly and in which direction does such a number change if you change one of its inputs a little? And if there are thousands of inputs in which direction must you shift all of them at once so that the number grows fastest or falls fastest? On top of that comes a practical question. Often the number arises from a long chain of simple calculation steps. You could change each input a little, one at a time, and see what comes out at the end. With a million inputs, that would mean repeating the whole calculation a million times. Is there a faster way? And how do you check whether a formula for these sensitivities that you derived or programmed yourself is really correct? The payoff with the answers, you know which adjustable knobs a result depends on most strongly and how small measurement errors in the inputs affect the result. You can replace a complicated function near a point by a much simpler one and estimate how large the error is. And you can compute the sensitivities even when the number arises from a very long calculation with very many inputs. Almost every method that learns from data needs these tools. How to work with this chapter. The sections build on each other, and every new term has its own subsection with an example. Expandable boxes contain background why a method works and where it comes from , derivations and proofs; you do not need them to read on. Try the exercises ★ to ★★★ yourself first and actually run the programs; the solution expands right below each exercise.

A computer evaluates long formulas step by step, and each step is a simple operation with a known derivative. A computational graph makes these steps and their dependencies visible. By the product rule, a product of factors has a derivative consisting of terms with factors each; so the formula grows with , while the function has only factors. With intermediate results, by contrast, the calculation stays small. After each step, you keep the current value and the current derivative and continue calculating with numbers, not with formulas. With the computational graph, derivatives can be computed mechanically, without rearranging formulas and exactly up to the rounding of the elementary operations. This is called automatic differentiation. There are two ways to combine the local derivatives forward, in step with the calculation, or backward, from the result to the inputs. Reverse mode delivers the derivative of a number with respect to all its inputs in a single pass, and this section shows why that costs so little. What automatic differentiation is There are three ways to get the derivative of a calculation. You can transform the formula with the rules; this is called symbolic differentiation, and by Section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 the formulas grow quickly in the process. You can evaluate the function at two nearby points and form a difference quotient; this is called numerical differentiation, it is only approximately correct, and Section 11 numerische ableitung und gradientenprufung.html stufe 11 examines its error. The third way combines the advantages of the other two. Automatic differentiation computes derivatives of a calculation by applying the chain rule to its computational graph it evaluates the local derivatives with the numbers of the calculation and combines them according to the sum over the paths. Automatic differentiation calculates with numbers, not with formulas, and therefore no expressions swell. It approximates nothing the result is the exact derivative, distorted only by the rounding of the individual calculation steps. And it works for every program that consists of elementary operations, even with loops and branches, because for the given inputs the program yields a computational graph. The step by step calculation in the example in Section 9.1 rechengraphen.html stufe 9 1 was already automatic differentiation. For 9.1 rechengraphen.html gl 9 1 , the previous section assembled the derivatives , and from the local derivatives, without multiplying out or differentiating the formula of . That was automatic differentiation, though still without a fixed procedure for the order of the calculation. The two following subsections give this order. ⁠ In short Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule with numbers to the computational graph; it is exact up to rounding and needs no formula. The cost Why is reverse mode so important? Because it delivers the gradient of a function with very many inputs almost as cheaply as the function value itself. The linear approximation of a number tells how it responds to small changes in its inputs each input contributes its partial derivative times its change, and the contributions add up to the dot product with the gradient. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, for steps of fixed length this dot product is largest in the direction of the gradient, which therefore points uphill most steeply and is perpendicular to the contour lines. If the number arises from a long chain of calculation steps, its derivative is a product of Jacobian matrices, that is, a sum over all paths, and reverse mode computes this product starting from the number with row vectors, so that it delivers all derivatives at once for a small multiple of the cost of a single evaluation. One principle behind all the results. Almost everything in this chapter follows from one principle close enough to a point, every differentiable function is linear.
